body: There are eleven people in a front room on a Wednesday evening and the heating is up too high. A woman of twenty-six, who has been coming for about a year and is generally the one who brings something, asks what actually happens to her grandmother, who died in a village where there was no church of any kind and no missionary had been in living memory. She asks it plainly, in the middle of the study, because it is what she has been thinking about all week. There is a pause of perhaps two seconds. The man leading says that we just have to trust that God is good, and somebody stands up to see about the tea, and the study carries on from the verse they were at.

Nothing happened in that room. Nobody was rebuked, no doctrine was denied, and if you asked anyone there afterwards they would tell you it was a nice evening. And yet something was settled in those two seconds, and everybody in the room understood it, and the woman never asked anything again.

The questions are not exotic. Why does God permit this. What actually happens to people who never heard. How do I square these two passages that plainly disagree. Why did nothing change when I prayed about it for six years.

None of those is a threat to anything true, and it is worth being precise about why. Every one of them is already in the book. Job is a very long complaint against the management of the universe, and it was not left out of the canon; it was included, at length, with the complaint intact and God answering out of the whirlwind rather than tidying the transcript. Habakkuk opens by asking how long he is supposed to shout before anybody listens. One of the psalms ends in darkness with nothing resolved and no comfort offered, and the Church kept singing it anyway. The historic Church has argued the rest in councils, in public, in writing, for centuries. The discomfort in that front room was never about the question. It was about somebody not having an answer and not feeling able to say so.

This band carries 121 frequencies. Teaching and prayer hold a stretch of their own, every station publishes its schedule before it airs, and the passage a track stands on travels with the track rather than with a title somebody could edit.

Publishing in advance costs something that is easy to miss. It means the awkward text arrives on schedule whether or not anybody in earshot is ready for it. A station cannot look at the room and decide to do Philippians this week instead of Job, and it cannot let a silence in the studio close the subject the way a silence in a front room closes it. Nothing can be quietly skipped, because the schedule went out before the broadcast did. That is the whole discipline, and the reason for accepting it is simple enough: a question that gets shut down does not go away. It goes underground, and it takes the person with it.

Nobody in that front room intended any of this, which is what makes it worth diagnosing rather than denouncing. Most rooms are quietly optimised for confidence. The person at the front is expected to know, has usually not been given permission to say that he does not, and can feel the evening tipping if he admits it — so the lid goes on, and it goes on faster the more the question deserved an answer. The same reflex runs the other way outside the church, where the loudest voices on the internet are certain in the opposite direction and equally unable to sit with anything open. Both rooms are frightened of the same thing.

There is a frequency on this band called The Logos, still in build, whose entire format is continuous Scripture rotation: the text, at length, without a personality on top of it. It is being built on the understanding that people who have stopped trusting the commentary have not necessarily stopped trusting the book, and that the shortest route back for a person in that position is the one with the fewest voices in the way.
There is an alternative to all of this and it is not held by bad people, so it deserves stating properly.

It is that some questions really are above our pay grade, and that trust is the mature response to a thing you cannot resolve. That is not a dodge; it is very often true, and one of the marks of a settled believer is being able to hold an open question without it costing him anything. But there is all the difference in the world between arriving at trust and being handed it as a lid. The first takes time and is usually the end of a long argument. The second arrives in under three seconds with a change of subject behind it, and what the asker learns from it is not theology at all. It is the tolerance of the room, which is a much smaller and much more useful thing to know.
The question was never the danger. The silence after it was.

A man of sixty-two who looks after a primary school keeps an envelope behind the sun visor of his van. It has been replaced twice because it went soft. On it, in biro, in no particular order and with no dates, are questions: about his brother, about a passage in Judges that he has never been able to get past, about why the year his wife was ill went the way it did. He has been adding to it since about 2014. He stopped going to church a good while before that but he has never stopped writing them down, and he has never once asked anybody any of them out loud, including the vicar who buries people at the school and is perfectly nice to him.
That envelope is not unbelief. A man who had finished with God does not keep a list for eleven years. He keeps a list because he still half expects somebody to be there to give it to.

It has to be said that a radio station cannot answer his questions either. It does not know he asked. It cannot look at Judges with him, cannot tell him why that year went the way it did, and cannot give back the room that closed over the top of him in the first place. Some of what is on that envelope has no answer available in this life, and any station that implied otherwise would be doing the same thing the front room did, only with better production.

But an answer was never quite what was missing. What was missing was a place where the question could stay open without costing anybody anything, and that is a thing a broadcast can actually provide. It will play the lament without hurrying to the resolution. It will read the chapter that does not tie up. Nobody is watching your face while it does, nobody is waiting to see how you take it, and there is no second of silence afterwards that you have to interpret. The question is allowed to sit in the room for as long as you need it to sit there.

So the asking is not an interruption to the programming here. It is nearer to being the point of it. The instinct to protect God from hard questions is understandable and it is not shared by God, who wrote at least one book of the Bible as a long argument, and who has never yet lost one.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial and it helps to know they are there. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children in it. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. Nothing on any of them requires you to have a position first.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 313.80 — The Ancient Paths. The name comes from Jeremiah, and the line is worth having in front of you: stand in the ways and see, and ask for the old paths, where the good way is. It is an instruction to ask. It is God telling people who had lost their bearings to go and enquire, in public, at a crossroads, rather than to keep quiet and hope it passed. The station plays in the musical idiom of the part of the world where those questions were first asked out loud, and it takes the long view, which is what you want from anything that is going to sit with you while you think.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. There is an account if you ever want one; it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So put HM 313.80 on if you feel like it, this afternoon or in a month or never. Bring the question you stopped asking, or bring none. Nobody here is going to ask you how you got on, and there is nothing after this paragraph that you are meant to do.
